sections.title: Recognition
sections.text: Russula cyanoxantha forms a 5–15 cm cap, convex at first, then expanded and often depressed in the centre. Its colour varies greatly: violet, blue, green, olive, grey and purple can occur together on one cap. The cuticle may show fine radial lines. The gills are white to pale cream, fairly spaced, sometimes forked, and notably flexible and greasy to the touch.

sections.title: Flesh and useful characters
sections.text: The stem and flesh are white; the flesh usually does not change colour when cut. The spore deposit is white to very pale cream. Flexible gills are a useful clue, but colour alone cannot identify a russula.

sections.title: Habitat and season
sections.text: This ectomycorrhizal species grows in broad-leaved and coniferous woods, especially near beech and oak, but also beneath conifers. It usually appears from summer to autumn, depending on the region.

sections.title: Lookalikes and safety
sections.text: Other colourful russulas can look similar; reliable identification uses several characters and, for some lookalikes, microscopic examination. DGfM and VAPKO list this species as edible, but acrid russulas can cause digestive symptoms. The absence of a volva and ring does not identify an edible species. Never eat a wild mushroom without expert checking.

traits: Cap 5 to 12 cm (up to 15), convex then flattened and dished; very variable colours, often mixed: greenish black, violet grey, blue green, lilac, pink, ochre, yellow, green
White then pale cream, often forked gills, flexible and greasy to the touch: they bend without breaking
White stem, 5 to 10 cm, solid to stuffed; no ring
White flesh · mild taste, reminiscent of hazelnut
White to very pale cream spore deposit
Under broadleaves and conifers, mostly beeches and spruces, from early summer to late autumn
safetyNote: DGfM and VAPKO list this species as edible. Acrid russulas can cause digestive symptoms, and several species look alike: have your collection checked by an expert. The absence of a volva and ring does not by itself identify an edible russula.
